text:
Text classification systems often struggle to balance speed and accuracy. This paper solves that problem by introducing a fast text classifier called fastText [P2_p1_c02]. 

The main idea is a simple text classifier that represents sentences by averaging word information, while adding n-grams, which are sequences of words, to capture local word order efficiently [P2_p1_c04][P2_p2_c03]. 

Regarding cost and speed, the paper shows the system is many orders of magnitude faster for training and evaluation than complex deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. It can be trained on more than one billion words in less than ten minutes using a standard multicore CPU [P2_p1_c02]. It can also classify half a million sentences among 312K classes in less than a minute [P2_p1_c02]. 

In terms of accuracy, fastText is often on par with deep learning classifiers [P2_p1_c02]. On sentiment analysis tasks, adding bigram information improves performance by 1-4% [P2_p3_c02]. Its accuracy is slightly better than some character-based convolutional networks, but a bit worse than others [P2_p3_c02]. 

As for limitations, fastText does not use pre-trained word embeddings, which can explain small accuracy differences compared to other methods [P2_p3_c02]. The sources do not contain further information about limitations.
